newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end up, trade quiet, Fed watch on.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end up, trade quiet, Fed watch on.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed slightly higher in extremely light trading as players were mostly sidelined, awaiting the pivotal meeting of Federal Reserve policy makers on September 24, analysts said.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended up 1/32 at 96-11/32. Its yield was at 7.04 percent.

Although prices moved just a notch, pundits noted the market was fairly anxious ahead of the central bank's Open Market Committee gathering as opinions on what the Fed will do next remained mostly mixed.
"There isn't much to say, except that everybody is waiting on the Fed," said Josh Feinman, global markets economist at BT Securities Corp.
"Everybody placed their bets basically as to what they think the Fed is going to do on Tuesday. And we're now waiting," the economist added.
The question brewing now is how the market will react and to what degree of intensity after the Fed announces the outcome of the meeting on Tuesday.
"There will likely be some market reaction to the announcement, one way or the other," Feinman said.

Most analysts agreed Treasury's yields have plenty of room to rise if the Fed decides to increase short-term rates by 25 basis points at the meeting. The central bank's currently target for the federal funds rate is 5.25 percent.
"We could see rates a little bit higher here," said Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.

Analysts said long-term rates as measured by yields on the 30-year bond could quickly move to 7.10 percent and then 7.25 percent if the Fed decides to tighten monetary policy. "That would be a significant back up," a trader said.
Pundits said yields in the short-end of the curve could back up even further if the Fed tightens.
If confirmed, such a move could bring the spread between the two-year notes and the 30-year bonds to around 70 basis points from the current 80-point level, they added.
However, if the Fed decides to leave rates unchanged analysts see prices rallying. But they said the rush to the securities could be limited.
"If they (Fed officials) don't go now, they'll probably go in the November meeting and the market will trade again on expectations," said a money market trader at a U.S. bank.
In a Reuters survey released this week, 17 of 30 economists expect the Fed to raise rates in September.

Of the remaining 13 respondents, seven projected a monetary policy tightening at the November 13 FOMC meeting, one called for a rate hike early next year and five saw the policy unchanged in the foreseable future.

Analysts said the lack of fresh economic data also contributed to the market's sluggishness on Friday. Volume was extremely thin throughout the session, with professional players dominating the market.
"We had a very quiet day here," said Marilyn Schaja, economist at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette. "The market is very much much focused on what the Fed may do next week."
The three-month T-bill rate closed up four basis points at 5.14 percent. The six-month bill rate rose two points to 5.28 percent. The year bill was flat at 5.53 percent.

The two-year note closed up 1/32 at 99-25/32, yielding 6.24 percent. The five-year note traded up 2/32 at 99-16/32 to yield 6.62 percent. The ten-year note closed up 3/32 at 101-4/32, yielding 6.84 percent.
